dossier.notes:
# x86-64-cross
## Notes
- A compiler, assembler and linker that build freestanding code for x86_64-elf instead of the host operating system. [d1]
## Setup
- x86-64 cross toolchain on linux | Build x86_64-elf binutils and GCC as the OSDev wiki describes, or use clang with --target=x86_64-elf [d1]
- x86-64 cross toolchain on macos | brew install x86_64-elf-gcc [d1]
- x86-64 cross toolchain on windows | Inside WSL 2, build x86_64-elf binutils and GCC, or use clang with --target=x86_64-elf [d1]

# limine
## Notes
- A bootloader with its own boot protocol that loads a 64-bit kernel in long mode with a framebuffer and a memory map. [d2]

# qemu
## Notes
- A machine emulator that boots a kernel image headless, with a serial port on stdio and a GDB stub. [d3]
## Setup
- QEMU on linux | sudo apt install qemu-system-x86 [d3]
- QEMU on macos | brew install qemu [d3]
- QEMU on windows | Inside WSL 2, sudo apt install qemu-system-x86 [d3]

# c
## Versions
- C23 | The reference treats C23 as the most recently published C Standard, so it is the main focus. [d4]
- C standard revisions | The reference covers C89, C95, C99, C11, C17 and C23. [d5]

# osdev-core
## APIs
- LIDT | The instruction loads the IDTR from a pointer to an IDT descriptor made of a 16-bit Size and an Offset. Offset is 4 bytes in 32-bit mode and 8 bytes in 64-bit mode. [d6]
- IDT gate descriptor | A 32-bit entry is 8 bytes. It holds an ISR offset split in two parts, a code-segment selector, a gate type, a DPL and a present bit. [d6]
- struct InterruptDescriptor32 | The page gives a C struct that starts with a `uint16_t offset_1` field and a `uint16_t selector` field. [d6]
- Page directory and page table | On 32-bit x86, each has 1024 four-byte entries, so each is 4 KiB. A directory entry points to a page table. [d7]
- Round Robin scheduler | It uses one queue. When the system timer fires, it switches to the next process. Each process gets a quantum counted in timer ticks. [d8]
## Pitfalls
- Set up a working GDT before the IDT. [d6]
- Any IDT entry that is not present causes a General Protection Fault when it is used. [d6]
- The IDTR Offset must be a linear address, not a physical one, because paging applies. [d6]
- The page table address in a directory entry must be 4 KiB aligned, because the low bits are used for flags. [d7]
- The CPU never clears the Accessed bit, so the OS must clear it if it needs it. [d7]
- To make a page a user page, set the user bit in both the directory entry and the table entry. [d7]
- Plain Round Robin has no priorities, so many low-priority processes can starve a high-priority one. [d8]
- A smaller quantum means more time spent on context switches. A larger one makes the system feel laggier. [d8]
## Notes
- The IDT has 256 vectors, 0 to 255. [d6]
- Serial ports are much easier to write drivers for than USB, and they are commonly used for debugging in early kernel work. [d9]
- QEMU and Bochs can redirect serial output to stdio or to a file. [d9]
- On x86-64, paging fully replaces segmentation for memory protection. [d7]
- The page lists a 20–50 ms quantum as a common compromise. [d8]

brief.summary: A 64-bit x86 hobby kernel written in Rust, booted by Limine and run under QEMU. Pure logic sits in a host-testable library, and a serial test mode reports results and exits QEMU. Only milestone 1 is planned in detail now.

layers.name: x86-64 cross toolchain
layers.whatItIs: A compiler, assembler and linker that build freestanding code for x86_64-elf instead of your host OS.
layers.roleHere: Provides the linker and binutils that link the Rust kernel for x86_64-elf, and clang or GCC for any assembly.
layers.whyChosen: A cross toolchain stops host libraries leaking into the kernel, which a plain host gcc would allow. It is better documented than ad-hoc clang flags.
pros: Nothing from the host leaks in
cons: Building GCC from source is slow
Easy to call the host compiler by mistake
layers.learnerCost: Learn target triples and how to check which compiler you are calling.

alternatives.name: clang --target=x86_64-elf
alternatives.pickWhen: You want setup in minutes, not an hour.

layers.name: Cargo
layers.whatItIs: Rust's build tool that compiles, tests and fetches dependencies.
layers.roleHere: Builds the kernel for a bare-metal target and runs the host unit tests of the library. A small script makes the Limine image.
layers.whyChosen: Cargo comes with Rust and runs host tests with one command, unlike Make or CMake, which need extra glue.
pros: Host tests run with cargo test
layers.learnerCost: Learn Cargo workspaces and a custom target file.

alternatives.name: Make
cons: Rust needs a cargo call inside
alternatives.pickWhen: You choose C as the kernel language.

assumptions: A workspace: no_std kernel crate plus a host-testable library crate

layers.name: Limine
layers.whatItIs: A bootloader that loads a 64-bit kernel in long mode with a framebuffer and memory map.
layers.roleHere: Starts the kernel in 64-bit mode and hands over the memory map and framebuffer, so you skip real-mode setup.
layers.whyChosen: It skips real-mode setup that Multiboot2 with GRUB leaves to you, and it hands over a memory map that a custom loader would have to build.
pros: Memory map and framebuffer on request
layers.learnerCost: Learn Limine requests and its config file.

alternatives.name: Multiboot2 with GRUB
alternatives.pickWhen: You want to see the mode switch yourself.

assumptions: BIOS or UEFI boot is fine

layers.name: Rust
layers.whatItIs: A compiled systems language whose ownership rules catch memory errors at compile time.
layers.roleHere: Writes the whole kernel with no_std, and the host-testable library of allocators and parsers.
layers.whyChosen: Rust's checks catch pointer bugs early and Cargo gives host tests. C has less to learn but gives no such safety net.
pros: Memory safety without a garbage collector
Library code tests on the host
cons: Borrow checker takes weeks to feel natural
layers.learnerCost: Learn ownership, no_std and unsafe blocks.

alternatives.name: C
alternatives.pickWhen: You already know C and want to follow the wiki line by line.

assumptions: You are new to Rust, so early steps stay small

layers.name: Frame allocator, paging and heap
layers.whatItIs: Code that hands out physical memory frames, maps virtual pages and serves a kernel heap.
layers.roleHere: Reads Limine's memory map, allocates 4 KiB frames, edits page tables and backs a heap for alloc.
layers.whyChosen: A bitmap frame allocator is the simplest to test on the host, unlike a buddy allocator.
pros: Bitmap is easy to reason about
layers.learnerCost: Learn page tables, alignment and flags.

layers.name: GDT and IDT
layers.whatItIs: Tables that tell the CPU which segments exist and which handler runs for each interrupt.
layers.roleHere: Sets a GDT, then an IDT of 256 vectors with handlers for faults and the timer.
layers.whyChosen: On x86-64 the GDT and IDT are required. Hand-written tables teach more than a crate, though a crate saves time.
cons: Wrong entries cause General Protection Faults
layers.learnerCost: Learn descriptor layouts and the interrupt stack frame.
assumptions: Set the GDT before the IDT

layers.name: Round-robin scheduler
layers.whatItIs: A queue of kernel threads switched on each timer tick.
layers.roleHere: Switches threads on the timer with a quantum of a few ticks.
layers.whyChosen: Round robin is the simplest fair scheduler and easy to test. Priority schemes add complexity that is not needed yet.
layers.learnerCost: Learn context switching and saved registers.

layers.name: Serial first, then framebuffer and keyboard
layers.whatItIs: Small programs that talk to hardware such as the serial port.
layers.roleHere: Serial (COM1) prints text and test results to QEMU's stdio. Later: framebuffer, keyboard and timer.
layers.whyChosen: Serial is far simpler than USB or a framebuffer console, and tests read it.
pros: Serial is a few port writes
layers.learnerCost: Learn x86 port I/O and the UART registers.

layers.name: QEMU
layers.whatItIs: A machine emulator that boots a kernel with serial on stdio and a GDB stub.
layers.roleHere: Boots the image headless in tests, and exits with a status code via isa-debug-exit.
layers.whyChosen: QEMU is scriptable and has a GDB stub, which Bochs and VirtualBox do less conveniently.

layers.name: GDB
layers.whatItIs: A debugger that stops and steps a program and shows registers.
layers.roleHere: Attaches to QEMU with -s -S to step from the first instruction.
layers.whyChosen: GDB connects to QEMU's stub directly. LLDB works but has fewer kernel guides.
layers.learnerCost: Learn break, step, info registers and x.

brief.howItFitsTogether: Cargo builds the kernel with the cross toolchain's linker and packs it with Limine into a disk image. QEMU boots the image and Limine loads the kernel in 64-bit mode, then jumps to its entry point. The kernel initialises the serial port and prints its results. In test mode it writes a status code to isa-debug-exit, so QEMU quits and the script reads the serial text and the exit code.

milestones.title: Toolchain setup and booting test kernel
milestones.outcome: Cross toolchain, QEMU and Cargo are checked, then Limine boots a kernel that prints over serial and exits QEMU with a status code. Later milestones follow when this is done.

risks: Host compiler used instead of the cross compiler
Wrong linker script so Limine cannot find the kernel
Rust nightly setup and custom target errors
Paging mistakes later cause silent resets
friction: Limine hides the boot process that Multiboot2 would make visible
Rust adds a learning curve on top of OS concepts
The docs dossier covers 32-bit paging and IDT layouts, but this kernel is 64-bit with different entry sizes
